clinicalPearls: An abnormally elevated upper lid or depressed lower lid position exposing sclera, giving a staring appearance
Thyroid eye disease is by far the commonest cause and may show upper lid retraction and lid lag on downgaze
Upper lid retraction with impaired upgaze and light-near dissociation suggests dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome
Other causes include prior lid or orbital surgery, facial nerve palsy affecting the lower lid, and cicatricial changes
Retraction causes ocular surface exposure with dryness, irritation and risk of exposure keratopathy
Management addresses the underlying cause and protects the ocular surface, with surgical lid lengthening for stable cases
reference.pathophysiology: Eyelid retraction reflects an imbalance between the lid retractors and their antagonists, or mechanical tethering of the lid. In thyroid eye disease, sympathetic overactivity and inflammation and fibrosis of the levator-Muller complex elevate the upper lid, while proptosis compounds scleral show. Neurogenic retraction occurs when dorsal midbrain lesions disinhibit lid elevation. Cicatricial and post-surgical retraction results from scarring that pulls the lid away from the globe. The resulting exposure of the ocular surface predisposes to drying and keratopathy.
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of lid position and margin-reflex distances
Thyroid function and thyroid antibody testing
Assessment of ocular motility, proptosis and pupil responses
Neuroimaging if a midbrain or orbital cause is suspected
redFlags: Optic nerve compromise in thyroid eye disease
Neurological signs suggesting a midbrain lesion
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause; retraction from active thyroid eye disease may change with disease activity, and surgical correction is reserved for stable disease with generally good functional and cosmetic results.
pitfalls: Overlooking thyroid eye disease as the underlying cause
Neglecting corneal exposure and surface protection
Operating before the underlying disease is stable
management: Treat the underlying cause: control active thyroid eye disease and address neurogenic or cicatricial contributors
Protect the exposed ocular surface with lubricant drops and ointment, moisture chambers, taping or punctal plugs to prevent exposure keratopathy
For active thyroid eye disease, manage the systemic thyroid disorder and use corticosteroids, teprotumumab or orbital radiotherapy as indicated
Temporise upper-lid retraction with botulinum toxin injection into the levator-Muller complex
Reserve surgical lid-lengthening (retractor recession) for stable, inactive disease
Monitor the cornea for exposure keratopathy and refer to ophthalmology/oculoplastics
